title: The Moonroot Inventory
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 41 · The Seventh Ring arc
content:
Severus knew something was wrong with the door before the door did.

He was standing in our kitchen, measuring dried thyme into a jar, when a thin smell of seawater moved under the back door. We lived nowhere near the sea. The closest thing to surf on our street was the way the grocer complained about the price of potatoes.

Severus stopped pouring.

“Your garden is leaking,” he said.

“Most gardens do that when it rains.”

“It hasn't rained.”

Then he opened the kitchen door.

There, between the brick step and the rosemary planter, lay a folded note written on blue paper. The edges were damp. Beneath the paper sat a parcel of tools belonging to Brasswatch Yard.

We had not ordered tools.

Severus picked up the note with two fingers. “I am beginning to dislike the implications of that square.”

“You dislike most implications.”

“I dislike the ones that arrive unannounced in my herb garden.”

The note was from Neri. It described an error at the Lanternwell: goods and messages passing through their intended Threadways but emerging with somebody else's deliveries. People remained safe. The doors still opened by choice. The consequences, however, had become inconvenient for every community attempting to rely on them.

At the bottom someone had added, in handwriting broad enough to qualify as a threat: NO DRAMA. JUST BRING A LIST.

Severus examined it.

“Toph?” I asked.

“Possibly. The penmanship has the subtlety of a broken door.”

I laughed. Then I remembered the medicine shipment due at the Moonroot Archive and stopped.

We spent the morning counting.

The archive's shelves had been supplied with magical texts, ordinary repair manuals, herbs, and donated paper. Severus insisted on separating each quantity by source and destination. He refused the idea of naming everything simply ‘community supplies.’

“Ownership is not a vulgar word,” he told the volunteer who suggested it. “It becomes vulgar when it is used to erase an obligation.”

The volunteer, a young archivist named Ellis, held up an unlabeled bag. “And this?”

Severus peered inside. “An outrage.”

“An ingredient?”

“A collection of ingredients. Those are not the same thing.”

I took the bag and found dried calendula tangled with rosemary and lavender. The plants were harmless. The combination, left damp, would spoil within a day.

Severus reached for a fresh envelope without being asked. It was the quietest kind of partnership we had learned: noticing the work and doing it without turning gratitude into a debt.

At noon we went through the Moonroot Door together. We asked before carrying the medicines. We signed the lot into the ledger. The door gave us the familiar feeling of stepping from one weather into another, and we emerged beneath the archive's pale trees.

Iroh was in Lanternwell Square with a crate of teacups.

Greg was trying to persuade him that no, a guitar case did not count as a teacup delivery simply because both were fragile.

“You may keep it in the tea stall,” Iroh said.

“Thanks.”

“Provided you learn to steep the leaves properly.”

“That's a rough contract, man.”

Severus paused at my side. “We appear to have arrived at an educational emergency.”

Iroh's eyes brightened. “Ah! A fellow expert.”

“I wouldn't go that far.”

“You have not tried the tea.”

“Precisely.”

I walked away before either man could turn hot water into an international incident.

At the notice board, Neri had pinned a diagram of the mechanism. A wheel was bent. The damage was physical and small, the sort of injury that encouraged people to dismiss it until the whole apparatus failed.

I understood more than I liked about that.

Severus came up behind me with two cups. He offered me the one that smelled of jasmine. I took it.

“What do you think?” he asked.

“The bell is counting obligations nobody has written down.”

“Bells do not count.”

“Then we should perhaps ask why someone built this one with a ledger.”

He looked at me for a long moment.

“I do wish,” he said, “you would stop making observations that require research.”

“It's an expensive habit.”

“It is a familiar one.”

We brought the ledger to the archive. Names had been written in six columns for years: not the names of travelers, but the names of whoever promised to return tools, replace food, or tell another district about a change. It was a record of responsibility, not possession.

A seventh column stood empty.

Ellis wanted to fill it with ‘Lanternweald.’

“No,” Severus said immediately.

“Why not?”

“Because a place cannot apologize.”

The answer landed harder than I expected. For years people had blamed houses, schools, ministries, and wars for things that people chose to do within them. Institutions carried responsibility, yes. But names in a ledger were how accountability stopped becoming weather.

Neri arrived with Maui and the bent tooth wrapped in cloth. Maui was managing a remarkable impression of a man who had no intention of lifting the entire building.

Neri told us the bell had rung three times.

Ellis went pale.

Severus went still.

I reached for his sleeve, where the fabric had begun to twist between his fingers.

“Not another emergency,” I said quietly. “Another repair.”

He looked at my hand. Then he eased his grip.

“The two needn't be mutually exclusive.”

“No. But we can choose which one gets the louder voice.”

For a moment he leaned close, enough that his forehead almost met mine. The archive was full of people and the unfinished argument about tea carried through the open door. He touched my wrist with one finger.

“Later,” he said.

“Is that an invitation?”

“An observation about the continued existence of evenings.”

I smiled. “An admirably romantic specimen.”

His answering look was so severe that I knew he was pleased.

We spent the next hour designing a record that could be read without magic and repaired without permission from any one person. Neri would take copies to the other districts. Toph could examine the metal. Katara could check the water. Greg would ask the questions nobody thought to ask because they were too busy being impressive.

The seventh column remained empty.

On our way home, Severus returned to the diagram one last time.

“There is something else,” he said.

“What?”

“Whoever bent that tooth did not do so by accident.”

I looked again.

Across the brass were three faint scores. Not tool marks. Measurements. Someone had tested it before the bell began to ring.

“Do you think somebody is trying to close the doors?”

“I think,” he said, folding the drawing into his pocket, “that somebody tried to improve them without asking the people who depend upon them.”

It was, I thought, a much more ordinary kind of danger.

And a much harder one to banish.
